articleTitle: High-Precision MEMS North-Finding System in the Whole Temperature Range with Honeycomb Disk Resonator Gyroscope
abstract: The MEMS north-finding systems (NFSs) has the characteristics of small size, low cost, independent of external information. This paper reports a high-precision MEMS NFS based on the honeycomb disk resonator gyroscope (HDRG). The two-position method is applied to improve the precision of the MEMS NFS. The test results show that the bias instability (Allan deviation) of the HDRG reaches 0.0031°/h with maytagging <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$(\pm 180^{\circ})$</tex>. Also, the north finding accuracy in outdoor environment, in vehicular environment and in the whole temperature range (-40°C to 60°C) reaches 0.18°, 0.31° and 0.19° respectively (<tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$L=28.18^{\circ}$</tex>, 5min). This paper provides a specific compensation for the zero bias observed during the cold start phase, the accuracy of north-finding after one hour of power failure is 0.18°.

articleTitle: High-end MEMS Gyroscopes: Challenges on Mechanical Design
abstract: In recent decades, significant advancements have been made in microscale electromechanical systems (MEMS) for sensing and actuation. Standard semiconductor manufacturing techniques have notably reduced both the size and cost of these devices. Additionally, integrating signal processing components with sensing and actuation elements have further minimized system size. Today, MEMS gyroscopes are predominantly employed for stabilization or altitude estimation applications, but efforts are being made to develop high-end devices that may compete with traditional high-end gyroscopes technologies. This work is part of the effort to achieve high-end performances. We will describe the challenges that must be faced, and the simulations necessary to assess these challenges. Then we will analyze the results and propose some ways to optimize a structure.

articleTitle: High-Precision Inertial Measurement Unit with Closed-Loop Fiber Optic Gyros operated by 1550nm 3-Fiber SLED Transceiver
abstract: We have developed a new generation of inertial measurement units (IMUs) that are based on 3-axis closed-loop fiber optic gyroscopes (FOGs) operated by a highly integrated SLED transceiver optical module, thereby eliminating several discrete optical components like depolarizers, fiber couplers or fiber-pigtailed photodiodes. Removing many fiber components lowers system costs but also reduces the number of splices of polarization-maintaining (PM) fibers, which dramatically simplifies the IMU's manufacturing processes and improves the system performance. The optical transceiver module is realized as a Butterfly (BTF) module having three PM output fibers with an integrated 1550nm superluminescent diode (SLED), a 1:3 beam divider, a 3-channel optical circulator and three integrated receiver photodiodes.

articleTitle: High-Performance 100g Accelerometer with Integrated Electronics in 3 cm x 3 cm form factor
abstract: This paper presents the development of a high-performance 100g single-axis vibrating beam accelerometer (VBA) with integrated electronics in a compact 3 cm x 3 cm form factor. The accelerometer demonstrates state-of-the-art performance suitable for inertial navigation under industrial temperature ranges and high vibration environments. The intrinsic performance, including bias and scale factor residual errors, is evaluated over a wide temperature range, and the stability is assessed using Allan variance. The device is subjected to rigorous environmental testing, including vibration rectification error analysis, to assess its robustness in dynamic conditions. These results underscore the necessity of precision calibration for maintaining high performance in harsh environments.

articleTitle: INS Alignment Duration Reduction Using GNSS Heading
abstract: In some application, INS must be fully operational, i.e. must provide its full performance as soon as possible. For some fast patrol boat operational scenario, the ship must reach the fattest it can a rendezvous point in a GPS denied environment. So the initial settling time may be an important parameter. This paper propose to reduce it by inserting external GNSS heading. High-grade Inertial Navigation Systems (INS) need an alignment procedure before they are fully operational. Generally, the alignment procedure is divided into two steps: • During the first step, a coarse alignment estimates attitude with sub degree error and heading with few degrees error. • As soon as the attitude and heading errors can be linearized, a Kalman hybridization filter is initiated during the second step to complete the alignment process and achieve a heading performance of around 1 milliradian (mrad). During the first step, the heading is typically self-estimated by the INS or can come from a stored heading alignment. In this paper, we propose an architecture that utilizes GNSS heading information to reduce the duration of the coarse alignment process. During previous navigations, an algorithm is employed to determine the bore sighting angles between the vehicle and the two GNSS antennas. This information is then utilized during subsequent alignment procedures, where the GNSS heading data can be used to initialize the heading of the INS. This paper details the operational case of alignment duration reduction on a fast patrol boat proving that alignment duration can be reduced by a 30% factor.

articleTitle: Compact Digital Symmetric MEMS Vibrating Structure Gyroscope
abstract: We present the performance of a compact digital symmetric MEMS vibrating structure gyroscope prototype (termed Discrete Digital Head or DDH) based on Silicon Sensing's inductive SGH03 silicon MEMS resonator [1]. The CRH03 Gyro module has evolved as a successful high performance gyroscope product available alone or in a DMU41 IMU product, however, only with analog control electronics. The purpose of this compact digital prototype is to directly replace the CRH03's used in DMU41 having also an explicit analog rate output to enable convenient integration and evaluation of a number of prototypes in a production DMU41 to gain high confidence that the desirable analog CRH03 performance, namely low ARW and high bandwidth, are maintained or improved with more versatile digital control electronics. A flexible FPGA-based implementation was selected with adequate resources to enable detailed insight into the fixed-point, discrete time control issues with a matched performance digital design. With this evaluation experience, a highly compact, low-power ASIC-based implementation such as the one being developed by InertialWave [2] would then follow for further reduced size and high volume production. The anticipated benefit besides a significant reduction in the size of the CRH03 and DMU41 IMU is to enable the benefits of digital control such as the well-known capability of a symmetric Vibratory Structure Gyro (VSG) also termed Coriolis Vibratory Gyro (CVG) to eliminate long term bias, e.g. 0.01 dph rate stability over a week [3].

articleTitle: Analysis and Suppression of Charge Accumulation Effect in Micro-Shell Resonator Gyroscope
abstract: In capacitive micro electro-mechanical system (MEMS) devices, the application of dielectric materials causes long-term charging problems in the dielectric layers or substrates, which especially affect the repeatability and stability of high-performance devices. Due to the long-term influence of the charge accumulation, the researches on influence and suppression are urgently needed. In this paper, the influence of charge acccumulation in Micro-shell resonator gyroscope(MSRG) is analyzed. Based on the AC bipolar voltage molduation, the suppress method of charge accumulation is conducted. In the following experiment, a 2mHz of frequency split drift is observed in tens of hours. After applying the bipolar voltage, the drift of frequency split is within 0.1 mHz, which means the 90% percent of frequency split drift is obviously suppressed.

articleTitle: Concept for System Performance Verification of INS/GNSS Solutions within GNSS denied Environments
abstract: The validation or qualification of navigation and localization systems with respect to position and velocity accuracy requires a precise reference called “ground truth”. Obtaining such a ground truth for a given local environment can be very challenging especially when GNSS is fully or partially denied due to spoofing, jamming, multi-path or other disturbances. This paper proposes a method for ground truth generation by combining LiDAR, inertial measurement technology and GNSS. The method is based on a two-step process. In the first step, the test area is precisely and automatically surveyed with an accurate LiDAR / INS / GNSS measurement setup (creation of a reference map). The second step is the verification, where the performance of the Device under Test (DUT) will be verified under difficult GNSS environment, the position and movement of the DUT can then be referenced independently of GNSS using the LiDAR / INS setup (now without GNSS) as reference, also called “Ground Truth”. Challenges raised in the paper are for instance the demand on excellent time synchronization, outlier handling and geo referencing of the INS / LiDAR data fusion. Experimental results of the verification method are presented, using a highly accurate DUT of the type iPRENA-M, an inertial navigation system, which is mostly used in defence applications where GNSS availability is restricted. The test trajectory extends to 40 km and includes significant sections where reliable GNSS is not available. The demonstrated performance is in the area of a few decimeters.

articleTitle: Experimental Measurements on RTK-Corrected Embedded Real-Time Navigation
abstract: Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) positioning is currently a state-of-the-art, high-precision solution within the domain of Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS). Its potential and limitations in military systems such as missile guidance or aerial drone navigation in difficult environments have yet to be fully explored. This paper investigates the performance of RTK in a series of controlled experiments, aiming to assess the accuracy of RTK-based position solutions. A particular focus is placed on examining the impacts of interruptions in correction data communication and increasing distances from the base station.

articleTitle: Performance Evaluation of Quantum Accelerometers for Space Navigation
abstract: Inertial navigation is an essential technology for space applications due to its autonomy from external signals and references. In space, inertial navigation systems utilize accelerometers and gyroscopes to measure changes in velocity and orientation, enabling a spacecraft to determine its trajectory independently, assuming the gravitational accelerations are well known. While conventional accelerometers onboard space missions often suffer from a large drift in the frequency range below 10<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">–3</sup> Hz, quantum accelerometers can provide highly stable and drift-free measurements of non-gravitational acceleration and consequently improve the spacecraft orbits. This work evaluates the performance of a 3-axis quantum accelerometer for space navigation. In this paper, we analyze the performance of such sensors onboard a spacecraft in a parking orbit around Earth in two scenarios of maintaining a nadir-looking orientation and having an inertially fixed spacecraft. To achieve this goal, we simulate a spacecraft in the low Earth orbit using gravitational and non-gravitational accelerations, and we develop an in-orbit performance model for Mach- Zehnder-type quantum accelerometers capable of calculating the detection noise, quantum projection noise, laser frequency noise, wavefront aberration bias, and contrast loss, together with external effects such as the impact of rotation, and gravity gradient for each individual measurement. Using this modeling and based on the propagated orbit, we simulate the measurements of a 3-axis quantum accelerometer along the orbit in two different scenarios: first, we assume the spacecraft to maintain a nadir-pointing orientation, and then we consider another scenario in which the spacecraft is assumed to be inertially- fixed. The results demonstrate that the nadir-pointing orientation introduces more noise, particularly in the along-track and radial directions, due to uncompensated rotation. However, in both the nadir-pointing and inertially fixed scenarios, quantum sensors still produce white noise, consistent with their drift-free measurement capabilities. Furthermore, the findings emphasize the critical role of sensor placement within the spacecraft. Positioning the quantum accelerometer along the main axis of rotation is optimal, as it reduces the impact of centrifugal forces and improves measurement accuracy. This is especially important for spacecraft in nadir-pointing orientations or during maneuvers. This research is the simulation and implementation of a low-Earth orbit, undertaken as a proof-of-concept. In the future, we implement this modeling for a trajectory from Earth to the Moon. We discuss the challenges, limitations, and potential solutions.

articleTitle: Validating the Integrated Motion Measurement of Flexible Beams
abstract: Integrated Motion Measurement of flexible structures extends classical strapdown navigation with inertial sensors including conventional aiding techniques. The goal is to improve the navigation performance and to detect structural deformations during the navigation process for advanced motion measurement applications such as structural health monitoring or control. This is achieved by distributing accelerometers, gyroscopes, and aiding sensors over the structure and by including dominant flexible motions into the navigation system model. This paper provides an experimental proof of the functionality of such integrated motion measurement systems (IMMSs) and further investigates several system-related settings and parameters such as additional sensor types, method and number of sensor placement, together with the influence of classical estimation aspects. It is based on a previous theoretical study [1], which provided simulative proof and a first system design.

articleTitle: Top-Down Derivation of Performance Requirements for Inertial Navigation Systems
abstract: This work describes a mathematically sound approach to deriving requirements on component level from top-level navigation performance requirements. Considerations focus on inertial navigation for aerial vehicles as a prominent application. Firstly, a probabilistic analysis establishes the general mathematical relations between error distributions in initialization, inertial measurements and navigation solution in a bottom-up manner. Secondly, top-level requirements on the navigation errors are formulated as inequality constraints for the relevant marginal probabilities. The accordingly reduced design space serves as the basis for a top-down requirement decomposition method. In a numerical example, the proposed method is illustrated for a glide bomb with tactical grade inertial sensors.

articleTitle: Can a Perfect Vibratory Gyroscope Provide a Drift-Free Angle Estimation?
abstract: A perfect vibratory gyroscope, i.e. free of mechanical imperfections, is expected to provide an estimation of the angular motion that it experiences. The classical analysis explains how the actual measurements can be processed to produce such an estimation. We revisit this analysis and confirm that its conclusions are indeed correct, although only over a disappointingly short timescale. We then show that these conclusions can be extended to a much longer timescale by carefully accounting for some previously neglected small terms.

articleTitle: Development of a Levitated Linear Accelerometer
abstract: Sensors for linear accelerations based on levitated microparticles are introduced. We compare the designs of two technology platforms for the levitation: optical and electrodynamical trapping. In both cases the particle position detection is done via an optical homodyne interferometric scheme and via spatially sensitive detectors, allowing for acceleration sensing in all three directions with a single test mass. For the electrodynamic trap a first benchmark measurement of acceleration noise floor yields 2 × 10–<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> m S <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$-2/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$</tex> in a frequency range from 20 Hz – 170 Hz. With the main factor being displacement noise in the detection system, ways for mediation of the current limitations are discussed, which enable sensitivity noise floor reduction by a few hundred-fold. Finally, first measurements of contributions to scale factor stability show values down to 14 ppm with no detectable drift within the measurement period of about 28 hours demonstrating the potential of such a sensor in terms of long-term stability.

articleTitle: A LIDAR/INS SLAM Method Based on the PHD Filter
abstract: To address the issue of significant localization errors in single-system SLAM under challenging environments characterized by feature degradation, lack of loop closures, and GPS denial, a LiDAR/INS integrated localization method based on the PHD filter is proposed in this paper. First, the method integrates the inertial navigation system (INS) with LiDAR SLAM and enhances the system's ability to handle complex data association problems through the PHD-SLAM framework. Second, a fusion strategy based on the cardinal-distance method is introduced to achieve tight coupling between INS and LiDAR SLAM, thereby improving the localization accuracy and real-time performance of PHD-SLAM. Additionally, throughout the entire localization process, the LiDAR SLAM system continuously compensates for the INS estimates from adjacent frames to reduce accumulated errors. Finally, experimental results demonstrate that, compared to other methods, the proposed approach significantly improves localization accuracy and real-time performance. Thus, this method can effectively maintain high localization accuracy in feature-degraded environments.

articleTitle: A Novel Temperature Compensation Method for the Current-to-Frequency Converter
abstract: Current-to-Frequency Converter (CFC) is a high-precision analog-to-digital converter widely utilized for current acquisition of quartz accelerometer in inertial navigation system (INS). However, the accuracy of CFC is rather sensitive to the ambient temperature, specially the dynamic parameters, due to the temperature characteristic of electronics in CFC. The measured data indicates that the temperature drift of CFC scale factor shows complexity and exhibits thermal hysteresis. To address this problem, a novel temperature compensation method combining hardware compensation and algorithm compensation is proposed in this paper. Hardware compensation is achieved by adding an adjustable current source whose output current varies linearly with temperature in order to compensate the linear part of scale factor temperature drift. As for the nonlinear part and the thermal hysteresis error of temperature drift, a temperature compensation model based on multiple linear regression with the fusion of temperature and temperature change rate information as independent variables is established to implement the algorithm compensation. The actual experoments demonstrate that the two-stage compensation makes the temperature coefficient of CFC scale factor drops from about 3.5ppm/°C to lower than 0.2ppm/°C, indicating a significant improvement in the temperature stability of CFC.

articleTitle: Data-Driven Gyroscope Calibration
abstract: Gyroscopes are inertial sensors that measure the angular velocity of the platforms to which they are attached. To estimate the gyroscope deterministic error terms prior mission start, a calibration procedure is performed. When considering low-cost gyroscopes, the calibration requires a turntable as the gyros are incapable of sensing the Earth turn rate. In this paper, we propose a data-driven framework to estimate the scale factor and bias of a gyroscope. To train and validate our approach, a dataset of 56 minutes was recorded using a turntable. We demonstrated that our proposed approach outperforms the model-based approach, in terms of accuracy and convergence time. Specifically, we improved the scale factor and bias estimation by an average of 72% during six seconds of calibration time, demonstrating an average of 75% calibration time improvement. That is, instead of minutes, our approach requires only several seconds for the calibration.

articleTitle: A Detailed Journey from Tactical to High-End Navigation-Grade MEMS Accelerometers at EMCORE
abstract: EMCORE has decades of experience in developing quartz MEMS vibratory accelerometers, beginning with tactical-grade devices and advancing to demonstrate high-end navigation-grade accelerometer performance. This paper explores the hidden challenges that arise in high-end MEMS accelerometers, particularly those based on frequency modulation (FM). We delve into the distinctions between cross-coupling and cross-modulation effects, which become prominent as the noise floor is reduced, and discuss how these effects influence accelerometer precision. Additionally, advanced techniques for temperature compensation are evaluated, including conventional calibration and temperature self-sensing methods. To further enhance system robustness, we propose a multi-mode operational scheme that leverages multiple independent operational modes for temperature and gradient compensation. Our experimental results demonstrate navigation-grade performance, achieving bias instability as low as 30 ng and a total error of 2 μg across the full dynamic temperature range. These findings highlight the potential of EMCORE's MEMS accelerometers to meet the stringent demands of navigation-grade applications.

articleTitle: A Novel Approach to Model and Identify Quadrature Errors in MEMS Gyroscopes by Finite Element Analysis
abstract: With MEMS gyroscopes striving for ever better accuracy and pushing towards performance grades, which have been dominated by FOG-sensors not long ago, the analysis and understanding of the several bias sources gets more and more crucial. One possible bias source is represented by the so-called quadrature error. It can be caused by structural imperfections. To deepen our understanding of the underlying mechanisms, we carry out extensive finite element analysis (FEA) for an asymmetric dual mass gyroscope and a symmetric quadruple mass gyroscope. The focus is on two possible manufacturing errors: random overetching on flexural beams and, to our knowledge for the first time evaluated on this scale, the bow of the wafer. Comparing the simulation results with measurements of physical sensors allows us to identify the bow of the wafer as a dominant error mechanism since they show good consistency regarding the characteristic distribution of quadrature error and frequency split on the wafer. The simulated values for quadrature error are consistently lower for the asymmetric gyroscope. In case of the bow, they are +/- 11.5 °/s versus +/- 61.8 °/s for the symmetric gyroscope. By better understanding how the quadrature error in the sensor arises, we are able to further reduce it in new design iterations, which is key on the path to higher performance grades.

articleTitle: High-Performance Triaxial MEMS Accelerometer for Applications with Harsh Environmental Conditions
abstract: This work presents the next generation of NG LITEFs closed-loop microelectromechanical (MEMS) accelerometer. The B–500 is a form-fit-function compatible accelerometer to the B– 295. Its performance targets demanding tactical and navigation grade applications. For use in harsh environments, a focus lies on an optimized vibration rectification error (VRE). Analytical considerations show the trade-off between velocity random walk (VRW) and VRE. The strategies used to achieve an exceptionally low VRE will be explained. For the analysis of the VRW, analytical models of the entire system are set up, which allow the different noise sources to be analyzed and the overall system to be optimized. As of today, we can report a root-mean-square (rms) bias residual error of less than 59 μg and a rms scale factor error of less than 57 ppm over a temperature range of -40°C to 85°C after accelerated lifetime tests. The Allan deviation plot shows a very good bias instability of about 1 μg at a cluster time of 400 s, while a VRW of about 15 μg/Hz is achieved. The VRE was determined with a vibration profile of 10.9 g rms in the frequency range from 10 Hz to 2 kHz. Excellent values of the vibration rectification coefficient (VRC) of less than 5 μg/g^2 can be reported for direct mounting without any shock absorber. This makes the B–500 ideal for industrial applications that require high performance under harsh environmental conditions.

articleTitle: Analyzing Show Jumping Horses by IMU- and GNSS-Sensor Fusion
abstract: Accurate kinematic data is crucial for sports performance analysis, yet many sports lack reliable systems for concurrent accuracy, reliability, and validity measurements. This study aims to develop and validate a sensor-based motion analysis system for show jumping horses, comparing it to a camera-based reference system and exploring improvements in data estimation, particularly for dynamic center of mass modeling. We conducted a validation study using a GNSS-IMU sensor fixed to the horse's saddle pad, measuring acceleration, angular velocity, 3D speed, and position. The sensor data was used to compute key parameters of the jumping stride, such as duration, length, and height of the center of mass trajectory during suspension, as well as take-off metrics. Simultaneously, a 3D motion capture system with 12 cameras and 37 markers on the horse was employed as a reference. Data from five horses performing 56 jumps over obstacles of varying heights and widths were analyzed. Results showed that jump duration and ground speed at take-off measurements were sufficiently accurate and precise, with errors comparable to reported within-horse jump variabilities. However, other parameters demonstrated insufficient precision, with error standard deviations generally larger than within-horse jump variability. The increasing root mean square error for center of mass curves indicated that a static center of mass model is inadequate for accurately representing the complex movements of a jumping horse. To address this limitation, we developed a dynamic vector model for sensor-based center of mass calculation, accounting for trunk and neck deformation as well as limb flexion/extension during obstacle clearance. This paper discusses the development and potential applications of this improved model, contributing to the advancement of equine biomechanics and sports performance analysis.

articleTitle: Tightly Coupled Integration as a Strategy for Robust Navigation: Civitanavi Systems' Approach
abstract: This paper presents the Dual Frequency Dual Constellation GNSS/INS Tight Coupling (TC) architecture developed by Civitanavi Systems, as a preliminary step towards implementing an Ultra Tight Coupling (UTC) navigation system. As part of its strategic development plan, Civitanavi Systems aims to design and manufacture proprietary GNSS/INS modules at various levels of integration. After a high-level discussion of the Dual Frequency Multiple Constellation (DFMC) GNSS/INS Tight Coupling prototype, the paper discusses the results of several tests conducted both in controlled environments and real-world scenarios. These results are compared with those obtained using Loose Coupling (LC) integration, highlighting the superior performance of the TC solution. The results presented are part of the GAUSSIAN project<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sup><sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">1</sup>Galileo AUthentication and GNSS/INS platforms for Secure and Safe services In Air Navigation and mobility (GAUSSIAN). This project has received funding from the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under grant agreement No 101120406..

articleTitle: Applying Method of Averaging to a Harmonically and Parametrically Excited HRG with FTR Control
abstract: In this study modeling and simulation of a hemispherical resonator gyroscope (HRG) is accomplished via linearization and method of averaging where electrostatic excitation is both harmonic and parametric. To the best of our knowledge this is the first example in the literature for an HRG averaged model both excited harmonically and parametrically. Averaged and non-averaged open loop models are simulated under the same system parameters with different time step settings. Averaged model responses are compared to the baseline non-averaged responses to validate the suggested model and the modeling approach. Additionally, energy based force to rebalance (FTR) control method is applied on the averaged model to show its applicability.
